data.content_ref: inline:The mechanism asserts that the dual-aspect rationality thesis — splitting theoretical reason (Popperian anti-induction) from practical reason (evolutionarily hardwired 'naturalized induction') — is 'precisely the result' of Erdős and Rényi's 1959 paper, and further claims that paper 'states this conclusion in exactly these terms.' This is a hallucinated citation. Erdős and Rényi (1959), 'On Random Graphs' (Publ. Math. Debrecen), concerns the binomial random graph model G(n,p) / uniform model G(n,m) and asymptotic properties of graph components. It contains no discussion of Popper, induction, rationality, biology, survival, or any dual-aspect theory of reason. By invoking it as authoritative support 'in exactly these terms,' the target introduces a false factual premise that is load-bearing for the claim's credibility. A reader relying on this attribution would be misled into believing an established mathematical result vindicates the philosophical proposal, when no such connection exists. The countercondition 'If naturalized induction can be shown to be reliable, it undermines the claim that induction is logically invalid' is already destabilized, but the deeper fault is the fabricated provenance: the argument's rhetorical force rests on a citation that cannot support it.
